stages.name: Observe
stages.instruction: Each dot is an atomic nucleus — the dense core of an atom. In a radioactive sample, every nucleus is unstable: it will fall apart on its own ("decay") at some random moment, giving off a particle. Sweep $T_{1/2}$ (this isotope's characteristic half-life), toggle LOG, and let the sim run past $T_{1/2}$.
stages.concept: $N(t) = N_0\,e^{-\lambda t}$, with $\lambda = \ln 2 \,/\, T_{1/2}$. $T_{1/2}$ is intrinsic to the isotope — it's why carbon-14 dates fossils ($T_{1/2} \approx 5730$ y), why iodine-131 tracers wear off in the body ($T_{1/2} \approx 8$ days), and why uranium waste stays hazardous for millennia.

stages.name: Experiment
stages.instruction: A mystery isotope's decay curve (bright orange) is drawn over the plot with three sample points. Tune $T_{1/2}$ so your simulation's curve matches within $\pm 5\%$.
stages.concept: Two isotopes with the same $T_{1/2}$ decay at the same relative rate. Fit is easiest on a log scale — matching slopes = matching $\lambda$.

stages.name: Evaluate
stages.instruction: No live simulation. Only three noisy measurements $(t, N)$ from a hidden sample are given. Compute $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \,/\, \lambda$ from the data and type it in. Peek reveals the true curve for $1.5$ s.
stages.concept: From any two readings: $\lambda = \dfrac{\ln(N_1/N_2)}{t_2 - t_1}$, then $T_{1/2} = \ln 2 \,/\, \lambda$. On a log-$N$ plot the slope is $-\lambda$.

labels.tip1: sweep T½, toggle LOG, let the sim pass T½
labels.tip2: match the bright orange target — try LOG for a linear fit
labels.tip3: compute λ from two points, then T½ = ln 2 / λ

1.1: T½ is the time it takes for half the nuclei to decay.
1.2: Toggling LOG turns the exponential into a straight line — the slope is −λ.
1.3: The dashed teal curve is the theoretical N(t); the solid orange is the stochastic count. They should agree on average.

2.1: The bright orange curve is the target isotope. Match its slope, not just its ends.
2.2: On a linear plot, T½ is where the curve crosses N₀/2. On a log plot, curves with the same T½ are parallel.
2.3: Δ shows your percentage gap to the target. Under 5% wins.

3.1: Pick any two points (t₁, N₁) and (t₂, N₂). Then λ = ln(N₁/N₂) / (t₂ − t₁).
3.2: Once you have λ, the half-life is T½ = ln 2 / λ ≈ 0.693 / λ.
3.3: Because the measurements are noisy, expect a small spread — the tolerance is ±3%.
